articles.title: Android's biggest open-source app store is officially refusing Google
articles.author: Hamed Paydarfar
articles.content:
Summary
- Google begins developer verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand; global rollout by 2027.
- Developers must submit IDs, pay fees and register each app; unverified apps get blocked for most users.
- F-Droid and NewPipe reject the program, calling it a privacy risk and a step toward a 'locked-down' Android.
Google's controversial developer verification program has officially begun rolling out today, September 30, in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. The program applies to certified Android devices, and Google plans to expand it to every installation source in 2027.
While Android's official documents proclaim that this will help reduce the spread of malware and "boost user confidence," developers have criticized Google's approach and refused to comply, including the team behind F-Droid, Android's biggest open-source app store.
Google's program turns Android into a "locked-down platform"
And F-Droid says other developers must also become "advocates for software freedom"
Under the program, developers are required to create a profile and verify their identity with Google if they want full app distribution. Along with the $25 registration fee, individual developers must submit a government-issued photo ID and proof of address. Organizations, on the other hand, need a D-U-N-S number, a verified website, and official documentation.
Further, Google requires each app to be registered individually and verified through a signed APK. There's a free account that developers can take advantage of as well, but it limits distribution to only 20 registered devices.
Apps from unverified developers will be blocked, although Google gives power users a workaround. Its "advanced flow" involves enabling Developer Mode, confirming that you aren't being coached, restarting and authenticating your phone, and waiting 24 hours. After completing all those steps, you're allowed to install unverified apps.
In its open letter against this program, F-Droid argues that Google is transforming Android from an open operating system into a "locked-down platform." It says accepting Google's changing terms and surrendering identity documents will only put alternative stores and indie developers at a disadvantage. Moreover, F-Droid unequivocally advises all developers against enrolling "now or ever" and calls on them to become "advocates for software freedom."
The team behind F-Droid is not the only one publicly standing against Google's new verification program. NewPipe's developers have taken the same position in their announcement. They consider the program a privacy violation and refuse to surrender their contributors' anonymity.
Today's rollout is limited to four countries, so F-Droid and other direct APK downloads are not yet being checked. However, once the developer verification program expands globally in 2027, many developers will have a harder time distributing their apps to newer, more casual users.
articles.summary:
Google has launched a mandatory developer verification program in four countries, requiring identity documentation and registration fees for Android app distribution ahead of a planned 2027 global rollout.

### Key Points
- The program is currently active in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand, with a full global expansion scheduled for 2027.
- Developers must provide government-issued photo IDs, proof of address, or organizational documentation to maintain full app distribution capabilities.
- Apps from unverified developers will be blocked by default, requiring users to complete a complex "advanced flow" process to bypass restrictions.
- Open-source platforms F-Droid and NewPipe have rejected the requirements, citing concerns over user privacy and the potential loss of Android's open ecosystem.

### Why it Matters
This policy shift signals a significant move toward a more controlled Android environment, potentially limiting the reach of independent developers and alternative app stores. By centralizing distribution authority, Google aims to curb malware, but critics argue the move compromises software freedom and forces developers to sacrifice anonymity.

articles.title: I tested Eufy's E50, and it has everything you need in a local security camera system
articles.author: harish.jonnalagadda@futurenet.com (Harish Jonnalagadda) , Harish Jonnalagadda
articles.content:
There's a decent selection of Wi-Fi security cameras available, and I tested various Reolink and Baseus models in the last two years. But if you need 24/7 recording and local storage, the best choice is to get cameras that can be plugged in and connect these to a dedicated network video recorder (NVR).
This is where the Eufy Security NVR System E50 comes in. It is an all-in-one system that includes an NVR, a 2TB hard drive, four E50 PTZ (pan-tilt-zoom) PoE cameras, and all the accessories you need to install the cameras. The entire bundle costs $1,199, but AC readers can get it for $839 by using code EUFYNEWPOE — that's a $359 discount on a subscription-free security camera bundle. The code is valid on Amazon as well if that's your prefer choice of retailer.
Let's go over the basics, because the E50 system comes with a lot of stuff. The E5 NVR is the center of the hub, and this is what you connect the cameras to, and store your recordings. It also has a 3.5-inch hard drive bay, and it comes with a 2TB drive installed out of the box.
If you're planning on adding cameras down the line (there's also an 8-camera version), or just need to store recordings for longer, you can take out the installed drive and slot in your own — the NVR holds up to 16TB drives. Just to give you an idea, the default 2TB drive easily holds three months' worth of recording when using all four cameras.
The NVR comes with HDMI and Ethernet connectivity, one USB-C and two USB-A ports. The defining feature is eight PoE ports, allowing you to connect eight cameras to it without any issues. It has enough power to drive all eight cameras (it has a 90W power brick), and you can easily set up the NRV and view footage from the cameras by connecting it via HDMI to a monitor — you don't get a monitor bundled with the box, but there is a mouse.
Then you get the four cameras, and all the accessories to mount the cameras. There's a water-resistant housing, positioning stickers, screws, and four 59ft (18m) Ethernet cables. I didn't need the cables as I have Ethernet cabling running outside, so I was able to connect the cameras relatively easily to the NVR and set everything up without any hassle.
Talking about setting things up, you will need to install the Eufy app to configure the E50 system. I would've preferred a web portal, but that isn't available, and you need to use the app or connect a mouse and monitor to the NVR and configure it locally over your network. The app itself has a ton of features, and it was easy to set up the NVR and configure the cameras. The power-over-Ethernet cameras need just the Ethernet cable to provide power and transfer data, and while it is a hassle to run cabling to the desired outdoor locations where you intend to mount the cameras, it's a one-time chore.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
The E50 cameras have dual lenses — a 2K fixed lens with 180-degree field of view, and a 4K movable lens with 360-degree rotation with 65ft range and 5x zoom. With four cameras connected to the NVR, I was able to cover the entire outer area of my house. Eufy has a nifty OmniTrack feature that dials in on a subject when it detects motion, and it does a good job in this regard. You can set up familiar faces and exclusion zones with relative ease, and the cameras deliver clear footage even at night.
There's on-device AI as well (obviously) that's used to identify and frame subjects, and while I dislike shoehorning AI into every consumer product (these features existed before AI was a thing), I'll admit that Eufy has the basics covered. The E50 system gets multi-device view, cross-camera tracking, secure transmission of video feeds, and alert schedules.
In real-world use, the E50 did an admirable job; the cameras deliver clear footage, and I got instant alerts whenever they detected motion. Image quality is great, and I like using PTZ cameras because of the flexibility they provide — the secondary moving lens is great for tracking motion. I had no issues accessing alerts and camera feeds outside my home as well. Eufy finally uses end-to-end encryption (which is the reason I was willing to use these cameras), and while the brand took a while to rectify earlier mistakes, the E50 system doesn't have any security issues.
If anything, the only problem I have with the E50 cameras is that they don't integrate with the RTSP protocol. We moved to a new house last year, and I set up a DVA3221 NVR with 32TB storage and went with Reolink cameras. I did so as the brand has several cameras that use RTSP, and this allowed me to connect the cameras to the NVR and record footage with ease. Thankfully, Eufy says it is enabling RTSP in the coming months, and I will update this post once I use it with my NVR.
Look, if you're starting out and want an all-in-one solution with secure access, there's no doubting that Eufy did a great job bundling all the products you need. Oh, and if you want to add indoor cameras down the line, there's a Wi-Fi Module that lets you connect Eufy Wi-Fi cameras to the NVR, and that's good to see. Wi-Fi cameras are inherently more annoying to use — I hated the Nest Outdoor Cam — but they are a better choice indoors as you don't need to run cabling.
I get that even the discounted $840 price is quite a lot of cash to pay for a security system, but the E50 is designed to last, and it is more affordable in the long-term than using any Wi-Fi cameras that run on subscriptions, like Nest or Ring.
Not having to charge the cameras is a huge bonus, and you can be safe in the knowledge that all recordings are stored locally and not on a cloud server somewhere. You get actionable insights, Eufy's multi-view feature is pretty great in its own right, and the cameras deliver clean footage even at night. On the whole, it's a good choice if you need an all-in-one security camera system to cover your home and yard.
Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd.

articles.title: Why AI-powered romance scams are harder than ever to spot
articles.author: Rachel Feltman, Fonda Mwangi, Alex Sugiura
articles.content:
Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Earlier this month six men were extradited from South Africa for allegedly conning more than 100 U.S. women out of more than $6 million. According to the FBI, the men were members of a large organized crime ring that sometimes crafted and maintained elaborate romantic relationships to defraud their targets.
The idea of someone using romance to con you isn’t new; it’s practically a tale as old as time. But the Internet made it possible to implement these schemes from the other side of the globe. Thanks to the ubiquitous nature of online socializing and dating, it no longer sounds inherently fishy to fall for someone you’ve yet to meet in person.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Fangzhou Wang is an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of Texas at Arlington who studies online financial crimes. She says that now AI is the latest technological advance that’s making romance cons harder to spot—and easier to scale.
Thank you so much for coming on to talk with us today.
Fangzhou Wang: Thank you for inviting me.
Feltman: So how did you get interested in studying romance scams?
Wang: So initially when I get into the field of online scams, so my research actually broadly focuses on online financial crimes and how technology actually creates new opportunities for the offenders to target and exploit the victims in cyberspace. And over time, my work has somehow expanded from what I study in the Ph.D. into, you know, online scam more generally, particularly, you know, [the] human side of those scams. So how scammers actually use persuasion, trust and deception to influence people’s decisions. So this kind of, you know, progression of my research, you know, naturally lead me to online romance scam because this is very interesting scam and how people actually tricking the victims on dating apps, where in the same time financial exploitations is oftentimes built around this kind of, you know, interpersonal, loving relationships.
And more recently, I have also studied, you know, a little bit regarding to the aftermath of the scam, where you have money mules, money launderers and, you know, broader networks that actually help move those illicit funds. And in more recent years, I began to focus in on, you know, how online scam or online financial crime impacting, you know, different populations, specifically elderly population, which could be one of the most vulnerable populations in the societies.
So that is how my research actually progressed, you know, moving from online financial crime, online scam, to romance scam and, more recently to, like, money mules or scams against elderly populations and ultimately, you know, of course, leading me to understanding a more broader, you know, psycho-eco systems that may impact the victims and also the societies as general.
Feltman: Well, to take a step back, could you tell our listeners, a little bit about what kind of scams are, are out there these days that you’re studying?
Wang: Well, the current scam I’m currently studying is, of course, the first one is online romance scam, and the second one I focus most heavily on is going to be the Bitcoin scam, meaning that, how scammers actually utilizing Bitcoins or broader, you know, cryptocurrency systems to elicit, you know, fund from the victims, and how those scams can potentially impacting both the victims and societies.
And aside from the general online scams, I have been also studying, you know, a little bit regarding to cyberstalking and also cyberbullying as well, especially those against teenagers and also minors. And in addition, with regarding to a more broader, you know, abusive nature of cyberspace potentially, I also study a little bit regarding to “sextortion” and also a little bit regarding to, you know, how image-based sexual abuse can potentially be penetrated online and against, you know, different victims from different age groups.
Feltman: Could you give us some examples of common romance scams that we’ve been seeing lately?
Wang: Well, lately, ’cause, you know, online romance scam in general, you know, the scammers are trying to use fake identities to persuade the victims into giving up their monies by building a trusted relationships in the firsthand. So that is a very common online romance scam that we have been knowing in the societies. But however, in recent years, I wanna say online romance scam has been industrialized in a more Bitcoin or investment-based trusted scams that [are] happening online. Specifically, when the scammers are building trust with you first, and then the scammers are enticing you or luring you to go on fraudulent investment platforms where the scammers will tell the victims that, “oh, we need to build a wonderful future together. And in order to do so, we need to do the investment, or we need to invest on these platforms and accumulate our assets all together.” But in return, the victims will find out the scammers are actually building up the fake platforms by themselves to lure the victims to invest on. So in the end of the day, the victims are actually just investing their own money by putting the money just directly into the scammers’ pockets. So that is how the romance scam are gradually developing from simply just using persuasive cues into the scammers are industrialized their operations by building, like, an entrepreneur around their operations by, you know, luring the victims into the investment apps before, you know, they actually exploiting them voluntarily in some ways.
Feltman: So we’re not talking about, you know, somebody messaging you online and talking you into sending them some amount of money. We’re talking about, you know, big operations where they’re forming, in some cases, really, like, long-term online relationships with you. You know, there’s an entire operation then funneling you into giving them money in what seems like a business decision.
Wang: Exactly. I wanna more emphasize the online romance scam nowadays is developing more like an organized crime or more likely to be a white-collar crime, if you wanna say it more generally. So instead of just a petty crimes that impacting only a smaller portion of the victims, but, you know, the victims around the globe are impacted by this kind of scam. And we do not know exactly where majority of the scammers are coming from, but we just know they stay anonymized, they stay organized, they stay in a group and trying to get into as many victims’ mind as they can or even their bank account.
Feltman: So how do you go about studying romance scams?
Wang: So one area of my work actually examine how romance scam operates, so that is going to be the one central things I’m currently studying on. So I have been studying, you know, scam communications and offender strategies to understand how scammers actually use staged processes to construct identities, initiate, you know, relationships, build trust, and eventually, you know, transition into what I called a financial request or financial crisis. So this, kind of, help us to think about, you know, romance scam as a staged processes instead of just like one single deceptive messages, and then the victims just give out money. So it’s not like this way.
And most recently, I have been studying, you know, how we can actually prevent romance scam before the victimization even occurs. So one of my most recent projects [is] actually trying to dive further into the persuasion strategies used by the scammers, how the persuasion actually works into enticing the victims to fall into those crises. So the basic idea is very similar to a vaccine, if I use this example. So instead of, you know, simply telling people how scam actually exist, so we expose potential users or potential victims to weakened example of the persuasive strategies of the scammers that they could potentially be using during the scamming process and explain how those strategies actually work. So the goal is, of course, to cut the connection or cut the persuasion cues in the first place before the victims fall into the bigger traps. So the goal is, of course, to help people to recognize that or resist to those techniques when they encounter in a real relationships.
Some of my recent works also examine, you know, the role of AI in those scams, especially generative AIs. So they can potentially make it easier for the scammers to produce, you know, convincing messages—because nowadays, if we get a chance to interview an offenders in cyberspace, they’d probably be like, “We won’t be [writing] those prescam scripts by ourselves. We use generative AI to generate realistic images to target more people in the societies.” So, and they also use AI to generate those images and identities.
And of course, at the same time, our research also [asks] whether people can be trained or recognize manipulation regardless of whether deceptive content was created by [a] human or AI and which type of cue is more persuasive to the potential victims or the general crowd.
Feltman: What are your findings, tell us, about how people can avoid these scams and spot them?
Wang: Well, I wanna say, all of my research that I just described in the previous questions, they are all in progress. But what is actually surprising me is, you know, how difficult it can be to translate, you know, general scam awareness into actual resistance. Because people, when they hear about online scam or romance scam, they may even be able to list, right, those clear and obvious warning signs. But recognizing a red flag in those [in the] abstract is very different than actually being able to tell them in the actual conversations when they are having [them] with the scammers. And somehow, even though with those awareness already preexisted in their mind, they can still be very susceptible to those persuasions. So this is one reasons that, you know, a lot of scam awareness, so-called trainings, can be less effective than they actually think they can [be]. Because a lot of time, you know, the scammers, they will read our papers as well. So they will adapt their strategies as well, simultaneously, when our researchers and our societies begin to progressing against those scams. So that is one central findings of my research.
And another interesting one, from my prevention research, is that, you know, simply creating a sense of threat or fear does not necessarily appear to be the most important mechanism for protecting people—because we do not want to, you know, entice a fear from the victims without actually telling them what the scam is actually about. [This] does not reduce their online activities or sometimes may have more adverse effects on how they actually talk to people online. So what seems especially important for me is that developing people’s motivation and ability to resist the persuasion is more important than enticing just, you know, the simple fear—because that kind of mentality suggests prevention messages should go beyond just saying, “Romance scam are dangerous,” right? So they should teach people what manipulation and persuasion looks like in the actual conversations and what to do when they actually encounter those red flags.
Feltman: And what are some of the red flags that people should be looking out for?
Wang: From a researcher’s standpoint, I think, the first one is not going to be the broken grammar again—because, a lot of [the] time, when people are saying, “Oh, the scammers are using a broken English, or they are using a fragmented sentencing when they are chatting with you, it’s the sign of a scammer,” [but] nowadays scammers are now, they are using AI to generate, you know, sentences. So of course, the grammar is gonna be great. It’s awesome. It’s just like a native, speakers when talking to the victims.
But I wanna say the most important sign I want everyone to notice [is the] use of images and the videos—because you want the person talking to you online [to] show their behavior is consistent, meaning that the images and the videos needs to be always consistent, telling the stories. But, however, it’s very hard in today’s world as well because the deepfakes can always help the scammers to create whatever images and videos they want to create, even in a consistent ways. So although I wanna say it is a red flag, but in some other ways it’s, you know, the scammers, if they really invest into the scam, they probably can overcome this challenge as well.
And the third red flag I wanna mention is whether they will have a video chat or voice chat with you in a live settings. This is a common red flag that I always recommend people to do when they are trying to, you know, talking to strangers online, especially for a prolonged period of times. But, however, [on the] other hand, things always come with double-edged sword, right? Because with the deepfakes and AIs, the scammers can just embed a deepfake, um, software into their video chatting platforms, and then they can change their face, change their voice. So I wanna say, overall, in general, it’s just very hard to actually, like, completely eliminate the opportunities to encounter scams online, especially on the dating apps.
So I wanna say: always have somebody around you, so you can always talk, talk to them when you see anything [that] might be raising your red flags. Do not keep yourself in a bubble without talking to your friends or your families or your classmates, right? So always let people around you, like, really care about you. Tell them what is going on in these conversations, what’s actually raising your suspicions, and they might be the perfect individual that can help you to tell if it is a scam or give you more advice on how to talk to strangers on the platforms. So that’s my suggestions.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, and it sounds like, unfortunately we’re at a point technologically where no matter how real the relationship feels and no matter how much evidence you think you’ve acquired that it’s real, maybe if someone you’ve only ever spoken to virtually asks you for money, that should just always be a red flag, unfortunately. Maybe in the 1 percent of situations where that is someone who genuinely loves you asking for money, maybe they just need to be let down. [Laughs.]
Wang: Exactly. Another thing I think [is] it is also very important that the prevention does not always place [the] responsibility on the victims’ families alone. The dating apps, the social media companies, financial institutions, and the law enforcement also have important roles to play. So we should not simply just asking the victims, “How you can become better at detecting scam by yourselves online?” but ask, you know, how the platforms or how the general societies can make those scams harder to carry out in the first place.
Feltman: Absolutely. Well, thank you so much for coming on to, uh, talk to us about this.
Wang: Thank you so much for inviting me.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday to chat with the Internet’s favorite food foraging expert: Alexis Nikole Nelson.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. See you next time!
articles.summary:
Modern romance scams have evolved into sophisticated, industrialized organized crime operations that increasingly leverage generative AI to build trust and defraud victims through fraudulent investment platforms and cryptocurrency schemes.

### Key Points
- Organized crime rings now use generative AI to create realistic identities, images, and flawless communication to manipulate victims on dating apps.
- Scammers frequently lure targets into long-term relationships before funneling them toward fake investment platforms to steal money under the guise of building a future together.
- Traditional awareness training is often ineffective because scammers continuously adapt their persuasion strategies to bypass common red flags.
- Experts recommend verifying identities through live video chats, though deepfake technology is making even these methods increasingly unreliable for confirming a person's true identity.
- Researchers suggest that responsibility for prevention should shift from individual victims to social media platforms, financial institutions, and law enforcement agencies.

### Why it Matters
These evolving digital threats demonstrate that online financial exploitation has moved beyond simple petty crime to become a global, white-collar industry. As AI tools lower the barrier for entry, the ability to distinguish between genuine human connection and sophisticated manipulation becomes a critical challenge for both individual users and digital security infrastructure.

articles.title: Potato by air
articles.author: Nathan Edwards
articles.content:
The Wing Hummingbird 7000W-B delivery drone weighs less than 15 pounds. It has 16 propellers — four for horizontal movement and 12 for vertical — a top speed of 60 miles per hour, a carrying capacity of up to 2.7 pounds, and a delivery radius of about six miles. It is authorized by the FAA for beyond-line-of-sight piloting. As a feat of engineering, it is impressive.
Potato by air
The day the dads in my neighborhood discovered drone delivery
Potato by air
The day the dads in my neighborhood discovered drone delivery
So far I’ve mostly used it to send people potatoes.
It all started a few Sunday mornings ago when my neighbor Will added me and a half dozen other local dads to a group chat. I only recognized a few of the numbers.
“Anyone looking for dumb stuff to entertain the kids?” he wrote, under a video of a drone lowering a blue doggie bag into his backyard. He’d discovered that we were now in the delivery range for drone service Wing’s partnership with Walmart, and could get household items dropped onto our lawns in 25 minutes. “Hopefully liquor store will get on board soon.”
Ever since I saw the video of an Amazon drone dropping a package in someone’s pool, I’ve needed to know one thing: Do you have to order drone delivery to your own yard? I raised the question in the chat.
Will, a few minutes later: “Nathan I just ordered you a potato to see if I can send to other people. 8 minutes out.”
Two minutes after that, a neighbor named Rick: “Will just want you to know you’re going to get your potato first.”
Rick and Will had each scanned the list of deliverable items — over two thousand of them — and independently arrived at the same conclusion. “There is currently an air strike squadron of potatoes headed to our neighborhood,” Rick wrote.
At 12:14PM, a drone dropped a doggie bag in my yard. It contained a single russet potato and a bottle of water. Three minutes later, another arrived in Will’s yard, also containing a single potato and a bottle of water. (The water bottle seems to have been added as ballast; every Wing order I’ve placed came with one.)
Someone posted “The drones are everywhere.” Those of us who hadn’t met introduced ourselves. An apparently more practical dad named Jason ordered himself a pair of gloves. Dev, who lives in the next development over, was just out of drone range and could only watch in envy. Eventually, a storm rolled in and the potato drones tapered off.
My sixth-grader turned our sky potato into oven fries; Will baked his.
The wild thing — aside from the fact that you can just order a drone delivery to someone else’s yard — is that each potato delivery cost 82 cents. Total. Each order came from the Walmart Supercenter a few miles away. Wing is absolutely losing money on this. There’s no minimum order, there’s no delivery fee, and the prices are the same as in-store. Wing’s not even collecting sales tax. Welcome back, millennial lifestyle subsidy!
At these prices, if you’re not using drones to send potatoes to your neighbors you’re leaving money on the table. That evening, I remembered that my friend Bill had been going through a rough time lately.
I sent him a potato.
Okay, technically, Wing’s terms of service state “You will not use the Service to engage in any unlawful behavior, or to cause harassment, nuisance, annoyance or inconvenience to Wing, its users or any other person.” And I can definitely see ways you could abuse the system to do that.
While I lacked actual permission to land a drone potato in Bill’s yard, based on our relationship, I was confident I had spiritual permission. (This was confirmed a couple of days later when he asked me to drone deliver some candy for his kids. I sent the candy, and then another potato, and then the link to the Wing app.)
So what’s stopping someone from using this to harass people, beyond your own moral compass and the fact that they ask you not to? When I asked what safeguards the company had in place to prevent unauthorized deliveries, Wing spokesperson Jessie Poole-Strang wrote:
Wing has safely completed over 1 million residential drone deliveries, averaging thousands per day. Customers must be physically present for their first order, and every order requires a verified account and confirmation of a clear delivery zone. Just like traditional delivery or mailing a package, customers can choose to send an order to a friend or family member’s address that lives in eligible service areas. In the rare event a resident ever has a concern about a delivery to their property, our support team can help (support@wing.com).
Now, is drone delivery wasteful? If you’re only buying a single lightweight item — like a stick of deodorant, a bottle of sunscreen, or a potato — it seems more environmentally friendly than driving to the store. And as long as it’s subsidized, it’s way cheaper than DoorDash or whatever people use. I could see situations where it would be genuinely useful, especially if you can’t leave the house but you desperately need a bottle of ibuprofen and a Gatorade (for example). And of course it would be preposterous to DoorDash someone a single raw potato.
Of course, once you order more than a pound or so of stuff, that math goes off the rails. One afternoon, my wife ordered a box of frozen horchata mochi and a pint of gelato — among the few frozen desserts on the list. They arrived in two separate drones, three minutes apart, and each came with a small bottle of water. They held up surprisingly well during their 7-minute trips in the full Texas sun, considering the total lack of insulation. But it did feel silly to get two drones for two items.
That’s how they get you, of course. They hook you with convenience while hiding the true cost of the service. Drone delivery further squeezes gig workers in an already shrinking labor market, and it’s one more excuse for big companies to suppress wages. You don’t have to pay a drone, and you don’t have to tip it, either.
It’s been just over three weeks since we found out we had access to subsidized drone delivery. Aside from the two desserts and a couple of bags of gummy Nerds clusters, I’ve only used it to send potatoes to the dads. I sent three last week, plus one to myself to throw them off the scent. I’ve probably blown my cover now.
The other day someone — not me — escalated and sent Rick a broccoli potato soup. I’m pretty sure it was Will.
What have I learned from all of this? Well, I now know a few more people in my neighborhood. I’ve learned that drone delivery is way more useful to me than agentic AI has ever been. And that given the opportunity to airdrop subsidized potatoes to my friends, I’ll take it.

articles.title: New report finds that rapid expansion of tokenization is giving rise to new styles of investing
articles.author: Camila Grigera Naón
articles.content:
Many people on Wall Street expected tokenization—the process of turning assets into tokens that can be traded on a blockchain—to amount to little more than reproducing legacy financial products on a digital ledger. What has happened instead has been eye-opening. According to a new report from data analytics platform Dune, on-chain investors are also using tokenization technology to construct an around-the-clock financial system that defies the design of traditional markets.
This development has coincided with rapid institutional adoption of tokenization. Dune reports that the total supply of tokenized real-world assets has exceeded $34 billion in 2026, and major categories—including cash equivalents and commodities—have more than doubled over the past year. Tokenized stocks have grown the fastest, rising more than 2,000% as the number of active holders blew past one million, per Dune.
Rather than simply putting familiar financial products on blockchain rails, onchain investors are concentrating on individual stocks, trading equities 24/7, and using private credit tokens in decentralized lending.
“The way the market is wired is completely different,” Dune CEO Frederik Haga told Fortune. “The whole underlying architecture of these venues [is] different, and so that creates different trading behavior.”
Few crypto inventions have captured Wall Street’s attention like the promise of bringing real-world assets on-chain. What began as a niche effort to represent real estate, bonds, and equities as digital tokens quickly gained momentum as asset managers like Franklin Templeton and BlackRock created tokenized government money-market and Treasury funds.
More recently, companies like Robinhood and Ondo Finance have brought onchain versions of stocks and exchange-traded funds to investors outside the United States. Earlier this month, Nasdaq announced a $100 investment in Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, to continue building out tokenized stocks. Meanwhile, the Securities and Exchange Commission has opened a limited path for compliant U.S. venues to test blockchain-based equity trading.
The divergence between Wall Street’s vision and actual trading habits is most visible in equities. On Wall Street, passive index-wide investing reigns supreme, as more than 6,000 U.S.-listed ETFs now outnumber individual stocks.
But on-chain, users prefer individual companies. Dune estimates that individual stocks account for 81% of tokenized equities held in spot markets. The value of those holdings grew ninefold over the past year, outpacing tokenized funds and ETFs.
“While a lot of the world’s financial system today has become indices and packaged products,… when people trade on the blockchain, it’s to express themselves more, as opposed to passive investing,” Haga said.
The split is also clear in lending. In traditional finance, U.S. Treasuries are the standard backing for loans because they are considered safe and easy to value. But on crypto lending platforms, investors are more often depositing tokenized private credit, or loans to businesses that can offer higher returns. Dune found that credit assets make up about three-quarters of all real-world assets deposited in decentralized lending, while only a tiny fraction of tokenized Treasuries is used the same way.
Yield is one reason, according to Haga. Tokenized private credit can allow investors to earn interest on their holdings while using those same assets as collateral to borrow and fund other trades.

### Key Points

- Tokenized stocks experienced a 2,000% growth rate, with active holders now surpassing one million users globally.

articles.title: Shure’s latest MV6 Gen 2 microphone blends broadcast‑level sound with gamer‑friendly design
articles.author: daniel@windowscentral.com (Daniel Rubino) , Daniel Rubino
articles.content:
Windows Central Verdict
The Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2 takes an already well-regarded USB microphone and gives creators more control without adding unnecessary complexity. With excellent out-of-the-box sound, smarter DSP features, expanded audio customization, and Shure's century-long audio pedigree behind it, the MV6 Gen 2 delivers premium vocal quality for gamers, streamers, podcasters, and remote workers at a fair $169.99 price.
Reasons to buy
- +Excellent vocal quality right out of the box
- +Useful DSP features
- +New configurable auto-level and denoiser controls
- +Easy setup with no audio interface required
- +Thoughtful MOTIV Mix software
- +Fair $169 price
Reasons to avoid
- -Utility-first design lacks visual flair, especially for gamers
- -MOTIV Mix installer feels surprisingly old-school
- -Advanced users may still want more granular controls
Why you can trust Windows Central
There are plenty of USB microphones aimed at gamers these days, but few come from a company with the audio credentials of Shure. For more than 100 years, Shure has built microphones for musicians, broadcasters, performers, and recording professionals, with products like the SM58 and SM7 becoming industry standards along the way. During a recent briefing with me, Shure described the new MV6 lineup as part of its effort to bring that expertise to creators who want professional-quality audio without the cost and complexity that often comes with traditional XLR gear.
That's what immediately appealed to me about the new MV6 Gen 2 ($169). I've spent the last 15 years using microphones for the Windows Central Podcast, livestreams, media appearances, and interviews. I've used plenty of microphones from Razer, HyperX, Blue, and others, but somehow this was my first extended experience with a Shure. After several weeks of testing, including an appearance on TWiT Episode 1101 where I received compliments on the audio quality afterward, I can see why the company has such a strong reputation among podcasters and broadcasters.
The MV6 Gen 2 may be marketed as a gaming microphone, but after using it, that label feels a little too narrow. This is a microphone for anyone who wants better voice quality without needing an audio interface, mixer, XLR cables, or a degree in audio engineering.
I've been part of Windows Central since 2007, having reviewed and covered many keyboards, gaming accessories, laptops, and PCs from all sorts of companies from the perspective of a Windows enthusiast and unabashed PC lover. I also run this site and have seen a lot in nearly 20 years here!
Shure had no input, nor did it see the contents of this review, prior to publication.
What's new with the Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2?
I didn't review the original MV6, but most reviews of the first-generation model praised its strong audio quality, easy setup, and excellent value while noting that customization was relatively limited compared to some competitors.
Shure appears to have taken that feedback seriously.
The second-generation MV6 focuses primarily on expanding user control through software and onboard DSP processing rather than reinventing the hardware itself. The microphone still ships with Shure's "sounds great out of the box" philosophy, but users now have significantly more flexibility if they want to fine-tune their audio.
New features include:
- Adjustable Auto Level controls with configurable target levels
- New Adaptation Rate settings that determine how quickly gain recovers after volume spikes
- Adjustable Real-Time Denoiser intensity
- New Speech, Singing, and Instrument presets
- A full 5-band EQ for advanced tuning
- White and black color options
- A longer included USB-C cable
- The ability to disable the microphone's touch-sensitive mute button
- Enhanced DSP processing and customization through the MOTIV Mix software suite
Perhaps most importantly, Shure accomplished this without turning the MV6 into a microphone that demands constant tweaking.
During my briefing, product manager T Banks repeatedly emphasized that users shouldn't need to understand gain staging, EQ curves, or audio engineering to get excellent results. The advanced controls are there if you want them, but the microphone is designed to sound great from the moment it's plugged in.
Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2: Price and specifications
At $169, the MV6 Gen 2 lands squarely in one of the most competitive segments of the USB microphone market.
That's a price bracket occupied by products like the Razer Seiren V3 Chroma 32-bit and HyperX QuadCast 2 S, both of which offer feature-rich experiences and recognizable gaming branding. The Shure takes a different approach. Instead of trying to out-RGB the competition, it leans heavily on audio quality, DSP processing, and the company's professional heritage.
On paper, the specifications are solid:
- Dynamic cardioid microphone
- USB-C connectivity
- 24-bit / 48 kHz audio
- Adjustable Auto Level processing
- Real-Time Denoiser
- Digital Popper Stopper
- High-pass filter
- 5-band EQ
- 3.5mm monitoring jack
- Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android support
Basically, these are all the things I want and need in a mic, and none of the extra stuff that I don't.
Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2: Design and setup
The MV6 Gen 2 won't be mistaken for a gaming centerpiece.
Compared to the RGB-heavy HyperX QuadCast 2 S or the eye-catching Razer Seiren V3 Chroma, the Shure looks almost understated. The cylindrical design, compact desktop stand, and minimal branding prioritize functionality over personality.
Personally, I like that approach, but I also like glowy things.
The MV6 disappears into the background during video calls and recordings rather than demanding attention. It feels more like a professional tool than a gaming accessory.
Setup is about as painless as USB microphones get. Connect the included USB-C cable, select the device in Windows, and start talking.
One of the more interesting insights from my conversation with Shure involved the company's decision to omit XLR entirely. Shure believes many creators are paying extra for XLR connectivity (like the $249 Razer Seiren V3 Pro) they never actually use. By focusing exclusively on USB and investing heavily in onboard DSP, the company was able to keep costs lower while delivering audio quality that approaches much more complex setups.
Having owned mixers and used XLR microphones myself, I completely understand that reasoning. For most people, this approach makes more sense.
Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2: MOTIV Mix software
The MOTIV Mix software is where many of the Gen 2 improvements come to life.
My first impression was admittedly amusing. The installer feels surprisingly old-school, almost like a utility from an earlier Windows era. Once installed, however, the application is refreshingly straightforward.
That's a good thing.
Companies often fall into the trap of treating audio software like a cockpit. MOTIV Mix feels more like a well-organized control panel.
One of my favorite additions is the ability to disable the microphone's touch-sensitive mute button on the side. The mute function works extremely well, maybe a little too well. I accidentally triggered it more than once while adjusting the microphone, so being able to disable it entirely turned out to be an unexpectedly useful feature.
Auto Level and Adaptation Rate
Auto Level is enabled by default and serves as Shure's answer to automatic gain control.
The new system allows users to set different output targets while also adjusting how quickly the microphone responds after loud volume spikes. According to Shure, this feature was added after feedback from gamers who found the first-generation microphone could take too long to recover after sudden loud reactions.
For streamers, podcasters, and excitable gamers, it's a genuinely useful improvement.
Monitor Mix
Monitor Mix lets users balance their own voice against system audio heard through connected headphones.
Anyone who records podcasts, livestreams, or interviews will appreciate having direct control over that monitoring experience without needing external hardware.
Tone and Advanced EQ
The Tone section illustrates Shure's overall philosophy particularly well.
Users who don't want to learn EQ can simply slide between Dark, Natural, and Bright tonal profiles. Those who want deeper control can switch to a five-band EQ and manually adjust key frequencies.
It's an elegant balance between simplicity and flexibility.
Real-Time Denoiser
One of the standout Gen 2 upgrades.
The original MV6 offered denoising, but Gen 2 allows users to adjust its intensity. Whether you're recording in a quiet office or trying to overcome computer fans, HVAC systems, or general background noise, the Denoiser provides meaningful control over how aggressively the microphone cleans up your environment.
Popper Stopper and High Pass Filter
The Digital Popper Stopper is designed to reduce plosive sounds caused by hard "P" and "B" consonants. During testing, it worked well enough that I never felt compelled to add an external pop filter.
The High Pass Filter can be set to 75Hz or 150Hz, helping reduce low-frequency rumble from HVAC systems, vibrations, and other environmental noise. Combined with the denoiser, it's surprisingly effective.
Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2: Audio quality
This is where the MV6 Gen 2 earns its asking price.
Throughout my testing, voices consistently sounded warm, natural, and broadcast-ready with remarkably little effort. The microphone's dynamic capsule does an excellent job focusing on the speaker while minimizing distractions from the surrounding room.
(You can listen to how it sounds above during my 3+ hour guest appearance on This Week in Tech a few weeks ago.)
More importantly, it sounds good before you open the software.
That might sound obvious, but it's becoming surprisingly rare. Many gaming microphones feel like they require software processing to reach their full potential. The MV6 Gen 2 starts from an already excellent baseline and simply gives you tools to refine it further.
That philosophy came up repeatedly during my conversation with Shure. I compared its audio approach to brands like Bose, where tuning and DSP should complement the product rather than compensate for its shortcomings. The expectation is that users plug it in and immediately sound better.
In my experience, that's exactly what happens.
Against the Razer Seiren V3 Chroma 32-bit, I generally preferred Shure's warmer, more natural vocal presentation for podcasting and spoken-word content. The Razer offers more visual flair and creator-focused effects (and the auto-tuning setup in Synapse is great), but the MV6 sounded more like a broadcast microphone.
Compared to the HyperX QuadCast 2 S, the Shure again prioritizes voice quality over spectacle. The HyperX remains one of the best-looking microphones on the market, while the MV6 feels more focused on delivering clean, professional audio.
Neither comparison is a knock against Razer or HyperX. Instead, it highlights how different Shure's priorities are. This feels like an audio company that happens to be making a gaming microphone rather than a gaming company trying to make an audio product.
Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2: Competition
The biggest competition comes from the Razer Seiren V3 Chroma 32-bit and HyperX QuadCast 2 S, both of which we've reviewed and given high praise.
If RGB lighting, aesthetics, and streamer-focused visual features are top priorities, either competitor may be the better fit.
If audio quality is the top priority, the MV6 Gen 2 presents an extremely compelling argument.
Shure's competitive advantage isn't lighting, software effects, or gaming branding. It's more than 100 years of microphone experience combined with DSP technology that originated from the company's broader professional audio business.
That heritage is difficult to replicate.
Should you buy it?
✅You should buy this if ...
- You want excellent audio without needing XLR hardware
- You podcast, stream, create videos, or appear in meetings regularly
- You value audio quality more than RGB lighting
- You want useful DSP features that work automatically
❌You should not buy this if ...
- RGB lighting and visual customization are important to you
- You want a microphone with multiple polar patterns
- You prefer software ecosystems as polished as Synapse or NGENUITY
Final thoughts
The Shure MV6 USB Gaming Microphone Gen 2 feels less like a gaming microphone and more like a professional USB microphone that happens to be affordable enough for gamers (or anyone who just needs a good mic that's not XLR-level).
For a first-time Shure user, that's probably the biggest compliment I can give it. After years of seeing Shure microphones dominate podcasts and broadcasts, I finally understand why so many creators trust the brand. The sound quality is excellent, the setup is effortless, the DSP features are genuinely useful, and the software gives you just enough control without becoming overwhelming.
My only real criticism is that MOTIV Mix lacks some of the visual polish and ecosystem refinement found in competing software suites. Beyond that, there isn't much to complain about.
At $169, the MV6 Gen 2 delivers exactly what Shure set out to achieve: professional-grade audio that simply works.
Engineered specifically for PC gaming, streaming, and content creation, the MV6 Gen 2 brings Shure's professional broadcast technology to more creators, including those purchasing their first dedicated microphone and looking to elevate their sound beyond a headset.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Daniel Rubino is the Editor-in-Chief of Windows Central. He is also the head reviewer, podcast co-host, and lead analyst. He has been covering Microsoft since 2007, when this site was called WMExperts (and later Windows Phone Central). His interests include Windows, laptops, next-gen computing, and wearable tech. He has reviewed laptops for over 10 years and is particularly fond of Qualcomm processors, new form factors, and thin-and-light PCs. Before all this tech stuff, he worked on a Ph.D. in linguistics studying brain and syntax, performed polysomnographs in NYC, and was a motion-picture operator for 17 years.

articles.title: FBI hunting the hackers who stole its employees' sensitive data
articles.author: Jenna McLaughlin
articles.content:
FBI hunting the hackers who stole its employees' sensitive data
In a video posted on social media, the assistant director of the FBI's cyber division, Brett Leatherman, vowed Tuesday to hunt down the members of a cybercriminal group going by the name of ShinyHunters, the same group that last week claimed to steal reams of sensitive data from the FBI itself.
"You know how to find us, and we know how to find you," Leatherman said in the video, encouraging the prolific group of loosely connected data extortionists to come forward and share information or face the consequences. "I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours."
The FBI says it is "aggressively" investigating the breach and how hackers got ahold of sensitive FBI employment information, including whether the hackers got into third-party software or the FBI's own internal systems. In a statement emailed to NPR, a FBI spokesperson said the bureau is working "around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs.gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted."
It's still unclear how much information was stolen, though media organizations and threat intelligence researchers have already verified the authenticity of some of the stolen materials. Meanwhile, a defacement message was posted on the FBI's jobs website late last week where ShinyHunters took credit for the attack, and the site was temporarily taken down.
Current and former FBI employees familiar with the matter, who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because they feared reprisal for speaking about an ongoing investigation, said many employees first found out about the breach from media reports. They suggested there could be as many as several terabytes of text files in the data tranche, including FBI job applications, details on promotions, information on sensitive job postings, family details, medical data and more. Those same employees, particularly those who have retired, say there's growing frustration with FBI leadership, including FBI Director Kash Patel, about the lack of communication about the breach, exactly who is impacted, and how the FBI plans to protect its current and former employees. Some retired employees who worked undercover might need protection services like relocation assistance or even name changes if their data is exposed publicly.
The FBI told NPR it sent multiple "bureau wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting" of the breach" and that "the FBI treats the security of its own information and the safety of its workforce as top priorities."
One former senior FBI official told NPR the breach could be on par with the 2015 compromise of tens of millions of sensitive government employee records from the Office of Personnel Management. The U.S. government attributed that breach to the Chinese government and described it as a widespread espionage operation designed to identify potential targets for intelligence gathering.
However, unlike the OPM breach, there is more concern in this instance that the stolen materials will fall into the wrong hands or be otherwise weaponized, either by ShinyHunters or any number of criminal, terrorist, or nation-state organizations seeking to pilfer the stolen files. ShinyHunters has come out and said it never intended to leak the files, despite giving a deadline of Sept. 30 for the FBI to amend previously published press releases about the group that it argued were inaccurate, but that doesn't necessarily prevent further theft or exploitation of the data.
The bureau and its former employees are "bracing for impact" and assume that the stolen materials may be irretrievably compromised, according to the former senior FBI official.
But experts argue that the ShinyHunters members, which many threat intelligence researchers have previously identified as a loose collective of young hackers around the world, should also brace themselves for the FBI's response.
Cynthia Kaiser, the former FBI deputy director of the cyber division who currently leads ransomware research at cybersecurity company Halcyon, described the hackers as "reckless" for targeting the FBI, particularly knowing the FBI has a clear policy of not paying a ransom or negotiating with criminal actors. "When any threat actor targets the FBI directly, they should expect that the FBI is going to marshall additional resources to bring them quickly to justice," she wrote in a social media post.
While the FBI has promised to seek the information to make arrests against ShinyHunters hackers in the wake of this breach, it's unclear how imminent those actions might be.
The FBI's video posted on social media also featured a recently announced arrest of one alleged member of ShinyHunters in Amsterdam by the Dutch National Police, an operation the FBI thanked its Dutch partners for leading. However, that arrest preceded the ShinyHunters theft of FBI personnel data, according to the former senior FBI official familiar with the matter. It's unclear if that arrest served as motivation for the breach of FBI data and whether there was concern about potential retaliation following that arrest.
While the FBI has not shared any technical details about how the hackers got into its systems, Google's Mandiant published new research revealing that ShinyHunters is currently targeting a vulnerability in a human resources software tool called PeopleSoft, which is owned by tech giant Oracle. PeopleSoft is a tool used by the FBI, among other major clients in IT services, corporations, government, academia and beyond.
Google originally disclosed information about the vulnerability and its exploitation in June and revealed that while the company released a patch, some customers instead implemented protections like a firewall to attempt to prevent bad actors from exploiting it. Ultimately, ShinyHunters has managed to easily bypass those controls.
articles.summary:
The FBI has launched an aggressive investigation into the cybercriminal group ShinyHunters after the hackers breached the FBIJobs.gov portal and stole sensitive personnel data from the bureau.

### Key Points
- The cybercriminal group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the breach, which potentially exposed terabytes of sensitive FBI employee data.
- Stolen information reportedly includes job applications, medical records, promotion details, and sensitive family information.
- Mandiant research indicates the hackers may have exploited a vulnerability in Oracle’s PeopleSoft human resources software used by the FBI.
- FBI Assistant Director Brett Leatherman publicly vowed to track down the hackers, warning them to come forward before facing legal consequences.
- The breach has caused significant concern among current and former employees regarding the potential weaponization of their personal data by criminal or state actors.

### Why it Matters
This breach represents a major security failure that could compromise the safety of undercover personnel and sensitive government operations. The incident highlights the persistent vulnerability of federal agencies to data extortion and the significant risks posed when third-party software tools are exploited by sophisticated criminal collectives.

articles.title: Lean LaunchPad – The Next Generation
articles.author: steve blank
articles.content:
You’re reading a four-part series on how AI has impacted our Lean LaunchPad class and what we did about it.
Part 1: The Year AI Came For Us
Part 2: AI Killed the MVP – Long Live the IUP
Part 3: The World Outside the Classroom Changed, The Class Didn’t
This post: Lean LaunchPad – The Next Generation
Lean LaunchPad – The Next Generation
While AI accelerates product development and customer discovery, it doesn’t accelerate understanding, evidence or insight. Teams still need to discover who has the problem, how painful it is, who controls the budget and data, what outcome counts as success, what failure is tolerable, how the product enters the workflow, and why a customer will choose a startup over dozens of fast followers or internally built solutions.
Here’s how we changed the course design to embrace the speed of AI while teaching students to first think deeply about their business, then act quickly to build it.
It took all summer and lots of suggestions from the Stanford Lean LaunchPad and Hacking for Defense instructors, but at the end of our own discovery, we concluded that our redesigned LLP class needed to:
- Double down in the front end of the class on the rigor of understanding Stakeholders, Problems, Hypotheses and Connections
- Double down on AI for its rapid development/deployment, time-to-market speed up and ability to transform entire industries
- Replace the MVP as evidence of the Value Proposition with “Snippets” (Using a small portion of the initial untested product to test a value-proposition)
- Replace the MVP as evidence for testing the other parts of the Business Model Canvas with “Minimal Tested Canvas” tests.
- Make Product/Market Fit targets category specific
- Change the class tempo to move even faster
- Use Design Partners as evidence of Customer Validation in the second half of the class
- Change the language to embrace new class concepts
What’s the Same?
The redesigned class will keep team-based, experiential learning, Business Model and Value Proposition Canvases, Customer Development, hypothesis testing, field interviews, weekly evidence reviews, validating the problem before validating the solution, permission to pivot and time pressure.
We’ll Start with a New Glossary
Renaming isn’t just a semantic hack. Language matters. It shapes behaviors and actions. In the chaotic and uncertain search for a business model, being precise with students helps them understand if they’ve made progress.
Here’s the new language we intend to use in the revised Lean LaunchPad class.
Stakeholders: users, customers, influencers, decision-makers, economic buyers, regulators, data owners, security teams, saboteurs, etc. Anyone influencing the adoption of your product/service.
Initial Untested Product (IUP): For the first class meeting, this will be an AI-created product/digital twin that may resemble a complete solution but has not been validated with customers or stakeholders.
IUP snippet: A small portion of the IUP used to test one value-proposition hypothesis without showing the full product.
Partially Tested Product (PTP): By the end of week 4 of the class, teams using IUP Snippets will produce a partially tested product based on customer feedback to validate/ invalidate/ modify the IUP.
Product-Outcome Fit (POF): A replacement for Product-Market Fit. A more focused goal for AI-accelerated startups to focus on.
Minimal Tested Canvas (MTC): A replacement for the term MVP for testing the other parts of the Business Model Canvas. The smallest set of experiments that meaningfully tests the non-product parts of the Business Model Canvas, including customers, channels, revenue, costs, partners, clinical end points, regulatory paths, and key activities.
Design Partner: A co-developer who first provides feedback, data, workflow access, and real-world testing in exchange for early access, preferential terms, or influence over the product. However, the real metric for success will be when the Design Partner is using the product and getting value out of it. (Design partners can be end-users in companies, warfighters, etc. who can buy or influence a sale.)
Design Partner Validated Product (DPVP): By the end of week 9, using successively refined PTPs, teams will have a Design Partner validated product.
Minimal Viable Product (MVP): A term previously used to discover and iterate on the value proposition and other parts of the Business Model Canvas – no longer used in the Lean LaunchPad class.
What Changes – Class Tactics
We’ll split the class into two parts:
Weeks 1 – 4    Think Deeply – Stakeholder, Problem and Hypotheses Maps and Connections
Weeks 5 – 9    Act Quickly – with a goal to get Design Partners
We’ll double down on Customer Discovery.
For the first four weeks students, using IUP Snippets, will get out of the building and map Stakeholders, problems, hypotheses and connections. The goal is to quickly understand current behavior, workarounds, budgets, failure costs, and decision processes.
Students will be graded on the quality of their outreach, not on the success of proving their snippet correct.
We’re going to Replace Product/Market Fit with Category-specific Product/Outcome Fit Goals. We’re updating generic product/market fit to match how AI companies are being built. For each product category, teams will use AI-specific Product-Outcome Fit discovery and validation goals:
- B-to-B enterprise software teams search for Outcome/Agent fit. The customer can define acceptable work, the agent reaches that threshold in the target workflow, the organization grants the required permissions, and the old alternative is reduced or retired.
- B-to-C consumer teams do mass creation and testing, spinning up and testing many variants in parallel. The team finds a problem/need, target archetype(s) and behavior, acquisition and retention loop, and distribution path that survive repeated testing across variants.
- Hardware teams build digital twins. Simulations predict the behavior of prototypes closely enough to accelerate iteration, while manufacturability, reliability, supply, and deployment remain viable.
- Life science teams accelerate their Initial Untested Product with simulation and modeling tools and test clinical endpoints (therapeutics, diagnostics, devices, clinical trials), reimbursement and financing.
We’re Eliminating MVPs for value proposition discovery. We’ll enforce rigorous problem and stakeholder discovery via hypothesis tests, using Stakeholder Maps, the Value Proposition Canvas and Lean Experiment Cards. (These are tools I’ve used at Imperial College in London to teach teams to solve “Wicked” Problems.) Teams identify and test problems and stakeholder hypotheses. Then they use portions of their initial product, the IUP Snippets, to test core value proposition hypotheses. There will be no “full product” demos until discovery is complete. Where the old class iterated low-fidelity to high-fidelity MVPs, the new class iterates low-fidelity to high-fidelity value propositions and stakeholder maps.
We’re Encouraging Synthetic Interviews but testing them against live interviews. Teams will create artificial personas and run weekly synthetic interviews. Then they will compare these responses with in-person interviews, validating or invalidating the synthetic responses and feeding the live responses back to the LLM to make the personas and synthetic interviews more accurate. Note the direction of authority: the live interviews grade the synthetic ones, never the reverse.
Create the Minimal Tested Canvas (MTC). AI can generate a product faster than a team can test the other eight boxes of the canvas. The “Minimal Tested Canvas” returns the course to a week-to-week focus on discovery, testing and experimentation of all canvas components (other than the value proposition). It tests a team’s understanding of the regulatory process, spec sheets, demand creation and sales model, funding, organizational decision processes, etc.
Create formal pivot-or-proceed criteria for discovery. Teams state their hypotheses across the canvas, test the problem, test the solution with IUP Snippets, then face explicit verify-or-pivot gates: verify the minimal IUP, the customer segment, customer relationships, the channel, and the revenue model.
Because AI removed the natural pacing that building and MVP used to impose, the class now imposes go/no-go criteria explicitly so a polished product can’t substitute for evidence.
Make Design Partners A Team Goal. The team’s class objective is to get one or more design partners. The partner commits scarce resources: staff time, data, integration effort, permissions, test environments, changes to workflow and the ability to influence the product.
A design partner is evidence of Customer Validation. In 2026, when anyone will take an online meeting and pilots spin up in days, a design partner who commits skin in the game is the honest signal.
AI-Specific Class Additions
Test for Learning Debt. Any team member should be able to explain the customer, workflow, evidence, economics, and key contradictions without opening a laptop. Technical members should hear customer language firsthand. AI-generated work should be attributed, and teams will distinguish what the model produced from what the team verified. (This is especially important in discovery: what was the result of synthetic interviews vs actual interviews.)
User Interface. The Initial Untested Product has to have a polish that wasn’t previously needed. Stakeholders compare every interface to a chatbots UI/design now has a greater importance than a traditional MVP.
LLM Costs. Three questions that didn’t exist in 2011 when this class was created are now core canvas economics: What does running a LLM cost you, and what are your unit economics? And what does it cost your customer to run it?
Autonomy Permissions. Which actions will the customer allow? At what level of reliability and reversibility. Human intervention remains especially important during early deployment and for sensitive, irreversible, or high-stakes actions?
AI Model Portability Is Strategic. Most frontier LLMs have proprietary context, tools, workflow, evaluation, trust, and distribution. A startup should assume that its preferred model, pricing, latency, terms, or relative quality will change. LLM Model dependence is therefore a business-model risk, not only an engineering choice.
“Trust” Evidence Is a Potential Moat In many markets, the evidence needed to deploy safely is not overhead added after product/market fit. It is part of product/market fit. NIST’s Generative AI Profile treats trustworthiness as a lifecycle discipline of governance, measurement, and risk management. The FDA’s AI-device guidance similarly connects iterative improvement to planned validation, documentation, and impact assessment.
Defensibility, opportunity size, team, and funding. The team’s defensibility moat needs to be part of discovery — from data, to model, to team, to hardware. Opportunity size and market type: is this an incremental improvement or does this change or create an industry? Team capabilities: does the team have unique attributes, experience and/or insight — and who else is needed?
Textbooks versus Tokens – Students won’t buy as many textbooks they’ll buy AI tokens and design tools. So expect to spend money.
Risks
A Heavier Lift for Faculty. The existing Lean Launchpad class had a lot more moving parts than teaching “how to write a business plan.” Yet it succeeded and scaled because it prepared students for the world as it was. This class will raise the bar once again – for both students and faculty. I believe the outcome will be the same.
Achievement inflation. In the current Lean LaunchPad class students are already padding the number of interviews they complete. We write off all but the most egregious as “cheating in your entrepreneurship class is like cheating in your parachute packing class.” The goal of finding Design Partners now creates new avenues to inflate accomplishments. We’ll be emphasizing partners that help validate the business and lead to growth not demos.
Design Partners as a Metric for Validation will likely result in students finding local maxima instead of the highest peak. However, this is no different from what happens in the early stage of most startups. We’ll be giving students heuristics to how time pivots to larger opportunities.
Teaching Student Teams How To Sell. In the past, a Go-to-Market strategy was just part of the customer relationship portion of the business model canvas. While a few teams generated revenue or received letters of intent while in class, we discouraged them from selling because at that point they hadn’t validated your solution. But now? We believe that AI will sufficiently accelerate problem and customer discovery in the front-end of the class. The pedagogy going forward is about the ability to rapidly discover and rapidly validate in the era of AI. So “selling” is actually curricula. This is a huge departure from the original Lean LaunchPad.
Putting the pieces together
In the end, while we’re changing the tactics of the Lean LaunchPad class, its foundational beliefs remain unchanged: products succeed when they solve real customer problems/needs or create entirely new products that improve the lives of people, communities and businesses.
This new syllabus is itself a hypothesis that will be tested in Stanford’s Lean LaunchPad classes. I’ll follow up with a “What we learned” analysis of these changes. And there will be updates during the spring as we test this approach.
Comments, suggestions and your experience teaching with AI are welcomed.
We’re thinking of creating an educators guide and holding an in-person conference at Stanford / MIT on these changes. Let us know via comments or email if you’re interested.
I’ve been lucky enough to have been present at the creation of the last 50 years of disruptive technologies (semiconductors, computers, the internet, smart phones). None of us could envision how they would change the world. I can’t wait to see what my students are going to do with AI.
Puzzling through what happened to the class, the world around it and what to do next was a joint effort. Thanks to Steve Weinstein, Mar Hershenson, Jennifer Carolan, Chuck Eesley, Tom Byers, Eric Volmar at Stanford; Pete Newell, for feedback and at Imperial College Cristobal Garcia and Erkko Autio for the opportunity to teach the Stakeholder and Assumptions mapping tools in our Wicked Problems class.
Below is a draft of the updated syllabus for the students. As you read this, keep in mind the students are doing 10-15 Stakeholder interviews a week.

Attendance

Before Class
-  Set up your teams of AI agents to have specific expertise to help you sort through your discovery efforts (research, notes, synthesis, creativity, design, and so forth). Keep in mind discovery is your job, not the agents’ job. But they can be powerful assistants.
  - Last year’s team used Claude Skills and Gemini Gems, ChatGPT for market research and Replit to build websites, Granola and Twinmind for note-taking; created synthetic users with Listen Labs and Viewpoints AI to test against real customer data; summarized their research in Google NotebookLM or Notion, then used Perplexity to create their weekly presentations. This year newer/even more productive AI tools are available.

- Create the initial hypotheses for the other canvas components (demand creation, go to market, costs, revenue model, etc.)

- For potential software products, create Product Snippets (not Demos) to test specific hypotheses with stakeholders or use AI to create models or other artifacts
- Do at least 10 actual human interviews (record the interviews)
  - Each interview in the format of: a “hypothesis/experiment/expected result/actual result/path forward”
  - Note that Stanford students do not count as interviews. 50% need to be in person.
  - All interviews require that the person you interview give you permission to record the interview. This needs to be in writing and/or capturing the permission in the recording itself.
- Create 5 potential AI customer personas and interview them, then have AI analyze the answers and create a new set for actual interviews. What is the consensus view as determined by AI?

Week 1: Stakeholders, Hypotheses, Business Model, Snippets and Customer Development

Weekly Presentations:
